prose.hook: Zambia is landlocked, but water still defines its borders and its economy: the Zambezi forms a natural boundary with Zimbabwe, and Lake Kariba on that border holds the title of the world's largest reservoir by volume, at 180 cubic kilometers. Beneath the high plateau lies copper, cobalt, and a run of other minerals that anchor the country's exports, alongside the hydropower generated by all that water.
prose.physicalGeography: Zambia sits in Southern Africa, east of Angola and south of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and consists mostly of high plateau broken by some hills and mountains. It is landlocked, but the Zambezi River forms a natural boundary with Zimbabwe, and Lake Kariba along that same border is the world's largest reservoir by volume.
prose.climate: The climate is tropical but tempered by altitude, with a rainy season running from October to April. Periodic drought and tropical storms occur during that same wet season, from November to April.
prose.economy: Zambia is a lower-middle-income economy in sub-Saharan Africa and a regional producer of hydroelectricity. It has significant trade ties and infrastructure investment from China, and has drawn on IMF assistance to restructure its debt burden. The country has one of the youngest and fastest-growing labor forces in the region, though it also contends with systemic corruption and extreme rural poverty. Its exports center on raw and refined copper, gold, precious stones, and electricity, while its industries span copper and emerald mining, construction, foodstuffs, beverages, chemicals, textiles, fertilizer, and horticulture.
prose.peopleAndCulture: Zambia's population is made up of many ethnic groups, with the Bemba the largest at roughly a third of the population, followed by the Nyanja, Tonga, Lozi, Chewa, and numerous smaller groups; English is the official language alongside these. Protestant Christianity is the majority religion at over three-quarters of the population, with Roman Catholics making up about a fifth and small communities of Muslims, Buddhists, Hindus, and Baha'is among the rest.
